title: By the Time We Meet Again
content:
When Sophie arrived at the railway station, the platform was almost empty. A cold wind moved through the open doors of the waiting hall, carrying with it the smell of rain and the distant sound of trains leaving the city.

She had not expected to see Daniel there.

In fact, she had spent the entire journey trying not to think about him.

It had been three years since they had last spoken properly. Three years since Sophie had accepted a job in Paris and Daniel had decided to remain in London. At the time, neither of them had been willing to admit that their separation was not simply about distance.

They had been twenty-seven, ambitious, frightened, and convinced that love would survive whatever they asked it to endure.

It hadn't.

Or at least, that was what Sophie had told herself.

She was about to leave the platform when she heard her name.

— Sophie.

She stopped.

Daniel was standing several meters away, holding a dark coat over one arm.

For a moment, neither of them moved.

He looked older. Not dramatically different, but changed in the subtle ways that only became visible after years apart. His hair was shorter, his expression more serious, and there were faint lines around his eyes that had not been there before.

— What are you doing here? — she asked.

— I could ask you the same thing.

— I'm going home.

— For how long?

Sophie looked away.

— I don't know.

Daniel nodded slowly.

— That's probably a better answer than the one you gave me three years ago.

She felt the old discomfort returning.

— Daniel...

— I'm not trying to start an argument.

— Good.

— I just wasn't expecting to see you.

— Neither was I.

A train announcement echoed through the station.

Sophie tightened her grip on her suitcase.

— I should go.

Daniel looked at her.

— Will you have forgotten me by then?

She frowned.

— By when?

— By the time you come back.

She almost laughed.

— You assume I'm coming back.

— I hope you will.

For several seconds, they stood in silence.

Then Sophie walked away.

She spent the next few weeks in the city where she had grown up, helping her mother organize the family house before it was sold. She had expected the visit to feel temporary, almost like stepping into an old photograph.

Instead, everything seemed strangely familiar.

The café where she and Daniel had first met was still there. The bookstore where they had spent rainy afternoons was still open. Even the small park where they had once talked about getting married had changed very little.

Only they had changed.

One evening, Sophie found herself sitting alone in that park.

Daniel appeared without warning.

— Are you following me?

— I could say the same thing.

She smiled despite herself.

— You always did have an answer for everything.

He sat beside her.

— I wondered whether you'd come here.

— Why?

— Because you used to say this was the one place where you could think clearly.

Sophie looked at him.

— You remember that?

— I remember more than I should.

She lowered her eyes.

— I thought you had forgotten.

— I tried.

The words remained between them.

After a while, Daniel spoke again.

— How long are you staying?

— Another month.

— And then?

— Paris.

He nodded.

— Right.

Sophie studied his expression.

— What about you?

— I'm still here.

— Still working at the same company?

— No. I left two years ago.

— You never told me.

— We weren't exactly talking.

She looked away.

— No. We weren't.

Daniel smiled faintly.

— I've started my own design firm.

— That's wonderful.

— Thank you.

A silence followed.

Then Sophie asked:

— Are you happy?

Daniel thought carefully before answering.

— Most of the time.

— That's a very diplomatic answer.

— I've learned not to make promises about the future.

She smiled.

— Neither have I.

As the weeks passed, they began seeing each other almost every day.

They had coffee in the mornings and walked through the city in the evenings. Sometimes they talked about their lives apart; sometimes they deliberately avoided the subject.

Slowly, however, the years between them began to disappear.

One night, they stood outside the old bookstore.

— Do you remember the first book you gave me? — Daniel asked.

— I remember that you hated it.

— I didn't hate it.

— You said it was pretentious.

— I was wrong.

— You were.

He laughed.

— By the end of this month, you will have convinced me that I was wrong about everything.

Sophie smiled.

— Maybe by then, I'll have changed my mind too.

Daniel became serious.

— By the time you leave, will you have decided what you want?

She looked at him.

— I don't know.

— That's all right.

— Is it?

— It has to be.

She reached for his hand.

He held it.

Neither of them said anything.

The day of Sophie's departure arrived too quickly.

She had packed her suitcase the night before, but she had not told Daniel what she had decided.

They met at the railway station in the afternoon.

The same platform.

The same cold wind.

The same feeling that something important was about to end.

— So — Daniel said —, this is it.

Sophie nodded.

— I suppose it is.

— Have you decided?

She looked at him.

— Yes.

He waited.

— I'm going back to Paris.

His expression changed, although he tried to hide it.

— I understand.

— Let me finish.

He remained silent.

— I'm going back because I have unfinished work there. Friends. A life I built myself.

Daniel nodded.

— That makes sense.

— But I don't want to go back to the life I had before.

He looked at her.

— What does that mean?

Sophie stepped closer.

— It means that by the time I return here, I will have made some changes.

— What kind of changes?

— I haven't decided all of them yet.

She smiled.

— But I know one thing.

— What?

— I don't want to spend another three years pretending that I don't love you.

Daniel stared at her.

For a moment, the station seemed completely silent.

— Sophie...

— I can't promise that everything will be easy.

— I know.

— I can't promise that distance won't be difficult.

— I know.

— And I don't know where we'll be a year from now.

Daniel took her hand.

— Neither do I.

She smiled.

— But by the time we meet again, I want us to have tried.

He looked at her for several seconds.

Then he pulled her gently into his arms.

— By the time you come back, I'll have learned how to stop being afraid of losing you.

Sophie closed her eyes.

— And I'll have learned that loving someone doesn't mean giving up the life you built.

The announcement for her train sounded overhead.

She held him tighter.

— I'll call you when I arrive.

— I know.

— You'd better answer.

— I will.

She kissed him once before picking up her suitcase.

As she walked toward the train, she turned around.

Daniel was still standing there.

He raised his hand.

She smiled.

Neither of them knew exactly what the future would bring.

But perhaps that was no longer the point.

By the time they met again, they would have lived another chapter of their lives.

They would have made mistakes, changed their minds, faced new difficulties, and discovered things about themselves that neither could yet imagine.

And if they were lucky, by the time they met again, they would no longer be the two frightened people who had once believed that love required certainty.

They would simply be two people who had finally learned how to choose each other.
